locator.work: Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (with The English Physician Enlarged), new edn. 1850 — Project Gutenberg eBook #49513, public domain
locator.heading: Thyme

source_text:
IT is in vain to describe an herb so commonly known.

_Government and virtues._] It is a noble strengthener of the lungs, as
notable a one as grows; neither is there scarce a better remedy growing
for that disease in children which they commonly call the Chin-cough,
than it is. It purges the body of phlegm, and is an excellent remedy
for shortness of breath. It kills worms in the belly, and being a
notable herb of Venus, provokes the terms, gives safe and speedy
delivery to women in travail, and brings away the after birth. It is so
harmless you need not fear the use of it. An ointment made of it takes
away hot swellings and warts, helps the sciatica and dullness of sight,
and takes away pains and hardness of the spleen. ’Tis excellent for
those that are troubled with the gout. It eases pains in the loins and
hips. The herb taken any way inwardly, comforts the stomach much, and
expels wind.

evidence.summary: Modern evidence supports Thymus vulgaris for respiratory issues (coughs) and antimicrobial/inflammatory effects via thymol and carvacrol. Specific traditional uses like 'dullness of sight' or 'sciatica' lack direct modern clinical validation in the retrieved literature, though general anti-inflammatory properties are noted.

concordance.rationale: Modern evidence (PMID: 29785774, 29744941) confirms antimicrobial and antioxidant properties of Thymus vulgaris. However, clinical trials for specific historical claims like 'Chin-cough' or 'worms' are absent; only general respiratory support is plausible.
concordance.uncertainty: High uncertainty due to lack of direct clinical data for pediatric coughs or anthelmintic efficacy in modern humans.
caveats: Historical claims lack specific dosage data.
Safety concerns exist for internal use in children.
